storyPoints.label: Start
storyPoints.story: Two factors influenced my choice of direction: the place should have had high mountains, but shouldn't have been too far away. At the intersection of these criteria was Annecy. The start of the hike is separated from my place by about 6.5 hours and a chain of various types of transport. First, I'm going to Gare de Lyon.

storyPoints.label: Lac du Bourget
storyPoints.story: Then I'm taking TGV to Lyon — fast, comfortable, uneventful. In Lyon I transfer to a train to Annecy, which leisurely winds between the mountains and at some point goes along the shore of Lac du Bourget! Such a beautiful place, why am I going any further, should have stayed here...

storyPoints.label: Views from train
storyPoints.story: But in Annecy, another train is waiting for me. It's going to Switzerland, but I need to get off at a small station with a very long name: Groisy-Thorens-la-Caille. My goal is those mountains over there. Now I'll take a bus ride and finally start walking!

storyPoints.label: Real start
storyPoints.story: Aviernoz! I have one and a half liters of water (let's remember this) and a thirst for adventure. Opening Strava, mapy.com and off we go!

storyPoints.label: Fields and gardens
storyPoints.story: From the very first steps I got stung by nettles. I'm making my way along the gardens listening to the melodious chiming of cow bells.

storyPoints.label: Sandwich
storyPoints.story: The further I go, the better marked the trail becomes. Also got a call from the refuge where I'll be spending the night – the network connection here is excellent, one can télétravail. Another turn opens a view of the valley, lake and the city — I'll see this landscape many more times from different angles. A good place to eat a sandwich!

storyPoints.label: Cow band
storyPoints.story: The main musical instrument of these two days are the bells. However, the constant buzzing of dozens of flies that swarm around the cows is also mixed in with the angelic chimes. Poor cows!

storyPoints.label: Glacier Aviernoz
storyPoints.story: The sign and maps claim that there's a glacier. Despite the fact that no ice is visible, its presence is unmistakably felt from the sharp change in temperature. A minute ago I was melting in a 30-degree heat, and suddenly over a stretch of two meters of trail I feel like I'm standing next to an industrial refrigerator.

storyPoints.label: Calcites and martian views
storyPoints.story: Greenery gives way to karst landscapes. Glad that I'm not walking here in the rain!

storyPoints.label: First Mont Blanc!
storyPoints.story: The website of the refuge promises that in clear weather you can see Mont Blanc from there. So I sort of expected it, but actually I was absolutely not prepared to suddenly see on the horizon REAL mountains with snow caps.

storyPoints.label: Reached the Refuge
storyPoints.story: This is the flag of Savoy and finally the entrance to the refuge. Somehow I got here too quickly and easily. I still have plenty of time to look around and explore the area.

storyPoints.label: Piece of snow
storyPoints.story: For example, I can go to the grotto, which is located about forty minutes from the refuge. However, I turned back halfway because the whole road consisted of a karst leg-breaking desert. But I did see a piece of snow that forgot to melt and a sign about dangerous chickens.

storyPoints.label: Piece of snow
storyPoints.story: My only task for the remaining time before dinner was to choose where to look: at Mont Blanc or at the valley with the lake and paragliders. You can also watch people — some come here with huge backpacks and a clear intention to stay for the night, some packed very lightly and are already ready to run back down once they reached the top, many come in large groups or families, often with dogs too. The route is quite popular!

storyPoints.label: Aggressive chicken
storyPoints.story: Some notes about the refuge — it's the oldest one in France, operating since 1883, there are really some chicken, but there are no water at all! All the supplies are delivered by helicopter, so dinner and breakfast are quite expensive.

storyPoints.label: Dinner time
storyPoints.story: Everyone dines together in a large hall. First, the host talks about the history and the organization of the refuge, and then everyone eats! Bread and cheese, soup, tartiflette and even dessert. Very tasty!

storyPoints.label: Golden hour
storyPoints.story: After dinner, everyone goes outside to watch the sunset and settle in for the night. Many stay in tents, so not that many people slept in the house itself and I even got a separate room with two sleeping places.

storyPoints.label: Sunset
storyPoints.story: Sunset!

storyPoints.label: Moonrise
storyPoints.story: Of course, I really wanted to look at the stars in the mountains. But I first bought train tickets, and then checked the moon phase and it turned out that I had planned the trip right on the full moon. So no stargazing happened, but the moonrise from behind the mountain peaks was magnificent!

storyPoints.label: Night
storyPoints.story: I'm spending the night in incredibly luxurious conditions — in my micro-room there are not only two beds, but also a window overlooking the city and the glowing strip of sunset. No point to wait for the stars, so good night.

storyPoints.label: Morning
storyPoints.story: Woke up, stretched. Need to tidy myself up as much as possible (remember, there's no water on the mountain) and go watch the sunrise.

storyPoints.label: sunrise
storyPoints.story: Here it is!

storyPoints.label: breakfast
storyPoints.story: Breakfast is arranged simpler than dinner. There's a choice of cereals, bread with butter (the bread is very good). Drinks are free, unlike at dinner. No one eats inside anymore, instead everyone takes their trays outside and looks at Mont Blanc in the morning haze. It was so good that I only remembered about the photo when I had already finished eating.

storyPoints.label: Cliffs
storyPoints.story: Alright, let's go. I'm taking a farewell photo of the refuge and heading down. Mood is optimistic, water bottle is half full.

storyPoints.label: Cliffs
storyPoints.story: Since on the first day I walked to the top quite quickly, today I decided to take a longer route. I pass by cliffs that have been taken over by rock climbers.

storyPoints.label: Balmont (sud)
storyPoints.story: The walk down is slightly wavy. You can admire the landscape and drink water... Oh wait, better not rush with that.

storyPoints.label: Goose and chalet
storyPoints.story: I have a feeling that I'm seeing village geese for the first time in my life. They could knock you down and not even notice. Chickens cluck at the geese, geese honk back, cows melancholically glance at all this chaos. The bells are jingling...

storyPoints.label: Bikers
storyPoints.story: People are distributed along the route extremely unevenly. The chalet with geese was a popular place (there's an intersection and a good background for selfies), but after descending from the hill, I was alone again. This is my last chance to turn towards Navês-Parmelan. Or I can have a drink of water and continue walking the long road. (Okay, better just think about the water, there are about five sips left).

storyPoints.label: mont Lachat
storyPoints.story: Climbed another hill... A great place to reduce the amount of water left in the bottle by another couple of sips. By the way, I wonder how the cyclists who passed me got up here? The trail was somewhat non-existent, quite steep and crossed by tree roots.

storyPoints.label: signs in the forest
storyPoints.story: In this part of the forest there are few steep slopes, but lots of educational signs, and people look like they just went for a short walk near their house. They probably came from Dingy-Saint-Claire. But that's not where I'm going.

storyPoints.label: First Blackberries
storyPoints.story: Aaand I'm turning onto an untrodden trail again. There are fallen trees here, an unexpectedly steep descent, slightly crumbling and slipping underfoot, and — thanks to the forest fairies — blackberries! Good thing I didn't listen to the people laughing that trekking poles are for old people, now the poles help me not to fall when I climb for berries.

storyPoints.label: River fier
storyPoints.story: Waaateeeer! Clean, cool, of course I'm not going to drink it. There's still something splashing in the bottle, and there's not that much left to walk, I just need to climb over the mountain, but it's small, right? Right?..

storyPoints.label: mountain
storyPoints.story: I'm tired, let's be honest. I want to whine, and I want water, but if I drink all my water now, I definitely won't make it to the top.

storyPoints.label: more Blackberries
storyPoints.story: Good thing there are blackberries, giving strength and determination to keep walking. Or... determination to give up on the plan, the climb, and some hypothetical beautiful view of the lake and turn towards the village. I think I've had enough blackberries:)

storyPoints.label: signs of civilization
storyPoints.story: And here are signs of civilization! On the porch of a large old house stood an old lady, with whom we exchanged bonjours. She says, il fait chaud, and I say, yeah, and my bottle is empty, and I'm coming from thaaaat mountain. This wonderful woman was impressed and brought me a whole glass of water — cold, instantly fogging up in the heat...

storyPoints.label: Apples
storyPoints.story: Wandered a bit around the town, treated myself with an apple. I was looking for a water fountain marked on the map, but instead of a fountain I found a cheerful woman who immediately decided to help me:) The woman introduced herself as Anita, gave me some plums, and suggested we meet up in Annecy in the evening:) (and we actually did meet for a drink)

storyPoints.label: drink
storyPoints.story: Annecy!

storyPoints.label: drink
storyPoints.story: For the rest of the day I strolled around the city. Drank water from all the fountains, enjoyed the clear lake, views of the canals and streets filled with tourists. Nice place, I should hike from here again sometime!
